serpGaps: No top result treats AI features as a discovery case. The guides (Atlassian, Productboard, ProductPlan, Product School, Maze) teach generic interviews, prototypes and prioritization. None adds the checks an AI feature needs before design: is AI the right tool at all, data readiness, a model feasibility spike, evaluation criteria and the cost of a wrong answer. Only thin agency/service pages (zignuts, smartdev, lexogrine) mention 'AI product discovery', and they sell rather than teach.

Cagan's four big risks are explained everywhere, but nobody maps them onto AI. Value, usability, feasibility and viability each change for an AI feature: users must trust an answer that varies; feasibility depends on data and model quality, not only engineering effort; viability includes cost per call and US privacy rules (CCPA/CPRA, HIPAA for health data).

Continuous discovery (Torres, weekly touchpoints) and the timeboxed 'discovery phase' (agency pages) appear as rival camps on different pages. No result tells a seed-stage founder when each fits, or how a first timeboxed phase hands over to a weekly habit.
No guide gives a day-by-day timeboxed plan with an output per block. Productboard and Atlassian describe stages without durations. Design-sprint pages give 5 days but answer only one question.
Examples are thin or tool-promotional (Jira Product Discovery, Zeda.io on Product Hunt). No result walks one AI feature idea from 'the board wants AI' to a build/change/stop decision.
No result offers an exit gate: what must be true before delivery starts. A checklist template is the TOFU lead magnet the SERP lacks.

No result covers who should run discovery (product trio in-house vs a design partner) for a startup that has no researcher or designer yet. The AI overview's 'I asked 40 product leaders' (Ant Murphy, Medium) shows definitions vary, but nobody turns that into a buying decision.

outline.answerHint: **Product discovery is the work a product team does to decide what to build, and why, before it commits engineering time to building it.** (≤30 words)
points: Carry the 'product discovery definition' secondary here (see carrier). Give Product Talk's discovery vs delivery split and NN/g's 'problem space, frame the problem, gather evidence' view, both cited, in our own words.
Discovery is not a requirements document, a roadmap workshop or a research report. Its output is a decision backed by evidence.
Name the two forms the reader will meet: continuous discovery (a weekly habit) and a timeboxed product discovery phase (a project at the start). H2 5 resolves them.
One line on disambiguation: in ecommerce, 'product discovery' means how shoppers find products (search, recommendations). This guide is about building software products.
Bridge: 'If discovery is about deciding, the next question is what you are deciding about: four risks.'

outline.h2: Which four risks does product discovery test?
outline.answerHint: **Product discovery tests four risks before delivery: value (will people use or buy it), usability (can they figure it out), feasibility (can you build it) and business viability (does it work for the business).**
points: Credit Marty Cagan / SVPG ('The Four Big Risks'). Say who owns each per SVPG: PM for value and viability, designer for usability, engineering for feasibility.

Introduce the table in one sentence, then the 'Table:' caption line. Columns: risk, the question, the cheapest test (interviews, prototype test, engineering spike, stakeholder review), and a column 'for an AI feature' that previews H2 6 in one short cell per row.
Note in one sentence that IDEO-style models merge value and usability into 'desirability', and that SVPG keeps them apart for business products. That is why B2B SaaS teams should test both.
Visual: risk lens card (visuals[1]).
Bridge to the process: which order to test them in.

outline.h2: What are the stages of the product discovery process?
outline.answerHint: **The product discovery process moves through five stages: frame the outcome, understand users, map opportunities, test solutions against the riskiest assumptions, and decide.**
points: Answers the PAA 'What are the stages of product discovery?'. Use H3s for the five stages, with one output named per stage (outcome statement, interview notes and journey map, opportunity map, test results, decision memo).
Tie in the Double Diamond (Design Council, 2004): discovery covers the first diamond (discover, define) and the early develop phase. Cite it; do not redraw the diamond as the main visual.
Teresa Torres' opportunity solution tree as the map for stage 3 (outcome → opportunities → solutions → assumption tests). Explain it, cite producttalk.org, and do not reproduce her diagram.
Assumption testing: test the assumption that would kill the idea first, not the easiest one.
Visual: diverge-converge stage strip with the output under each stage (visuals[2]).
Bridge: 'These stages do not wait for a sprint boundary. Here is how they sit inside agile.'

outline.h2: How does the product discovery process work in agile?
outline.answerHint: **The product discovery process in agile runs as a second track beside delivery: the same team explores and tests ideas while it ships validated work, and only validated ideas enter the backlog.**
points: Carry 'product discovery process in agile' verbatim in the opener (see carrier).

Jeff Patton's dual track: two kinds of work, one team. Cite jpattonassociates.com ('dual track, not duel track'). Warn against splitting discovery and delivery into separate teams with separate backlogs.
Comparison table (intro sentence first): discovery track vs delivery track by question answered, typical output, cadence, who is involved, and 'done' signal.
Product trio (PM, designer, tech lead) and Torres' minimum cadence of weekly customer touchpoints (cite producttalk.org).

Practical hook for Scrum teams: discovery items get their own lightweight board, and a backlog item needs a validated assumption before sprint planning. Write this as advice, not as a rule from Scrum.
Visual: dual-track loop (visuals[0]).
Jira Product Discovery: one sentence, as a tool for capturing and scoring ideas, not the practice itself. Keep tool talk to this sentence and FAQ 5.

outline.h2: When does a timeboxed product discovery phase make sense, and how long should it last?
outline.answerHint: **A timeboxed product discovery phase makes sense at the start of something new, a new product, a big feature or a first AI feature; continuous discovery takes over once the team ships every week.**
points: Resolve the 'continuous vs phase' split the SERP leaves open. Phase: new product, new market, first AI feature, board or investor deadline, no customer contact yet. Continuous: a live product with a trio that can talk to customers weekly.

Durations from site facts only: a design sprint answers one question in 5 days; a full discovery phase runs 3–6 weeks with 10–20 interviews; our AI discovery workshop runs 1 to 2 weeks. Link the design sprint hub once (the post's ONE cross-hub link) when naming the 5-day option.
Signs the phase is too long: the team keeps researching to avoid a decision. Signs it is too short: no user saw anything.
Hand-off: the phase ends by setting up the weekly habit (a standing interview slot), so discovery does not stop at the gate.
Do NOT repeat the design-sprint hub's comparison table. Use one sentence and the link.

outline.h2: What changes in product discovery for AI features?
outline.answerHint: **Product discovery for an AI feature adds five checks to the usual four risks: whether AI is the right tool at all, whether the data is ready, whether a model can do the task, how you will judge its answers, and what a wrong answer costs the user.**
points: THE SERP GAP SECTION. Open with sourced stakes: Gartner (July 29, 2024) predicted at least 30% of generative AI projects would be abandoned after proof of concept by end-2025, due to poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs or unclear business value. RAND's 2024 report names five root causes, and the first is a misunderstood problem. Both are discovery failures, not engineering failures.
H3 1, Is AI the right tool? Start from the user task; a rule, a filter or better search sometimes wins. People + AI Guidebook (Google PAIR), 'User Needs + Defining Success'.

H3 2, Data readiness: does the data exist, can you access it, are you allowed to use it (CCPA/CPRA; HIPAA for health data; customer contracts), is it labeled or labelable? Gartner (February 26, 2025): through 2026, organizations will abandon 60% of AI projects unsupported by AI-ready data. PAIR: translate user needs into data needs.

H3 3, Model feasibility spike: engineering runs real inputs through a candidate model before any interface work. Do not give a sample size as a rule. Value here means quality, latency and cost per call.

H3 4, Evaluation: write down what a good answer looks like before design starts, and choose the precision vs recall trade-off (PAIR). Example: a support-ticket triage model that misses urgent tickets (low recall) hurts more than one that over-flags them.

H3 5, Cost of a wrong answer: map who is harmed and how the user catches and corrects it. This feeds the guardrails. Cite the NIST AI RMF 'Map' function: after mapping, a team should be able to make an initial go/no-go decision.
Wizard of Oz prototype: a person fakes the AI's answers so you can test value before you build a model. Describe it as a method with no statistic.
Visual: AI readiness check grid (visuals[3]).

Soft pain CTA at the end (first UP link if not placed in H2 1): 'This is the part most teams skip. Our AI product discovery workshop runs these checks with your product, engineering and data leads.' Link the hub.

outline.h2: How do you do product discovery in two weeks?
outline.answerHint: **To do product discovery in two weeks, split 10 working days into five blocks, frame, listen, check risks, test and decide, and end each block with one written output.**
points: Carry 'how to do product discovery' (see carrier). Write it as Ahmad's method in the first person ('I start by…'), with no invented anecdotes.

Ordered list (ol) of the 5 blocks. Days 1–2 frame: outcome, decision to make, existing evidence (analytics, support tickets, sales-call notes). Days 3–5 listen: customer interviews; on the hub we interview 4 to 6 users, so cite that range as our practice. Days 6–7 check risks: feasibility spike with engineering, plus data inventory if AI. Days 8–9 test: a prototype with 5 users. Day 10 decide: build, change or stop, plus the checklist in H2 9.
Who is in the room and for how long: the product trio, plus a business owner. The hub FAQ says about 2 hours a day for workshop participants; use that only when describing our workshop.

Make it clearly different from the hub's 4-step workshop: label blocks by the question they answer, not by the hub's step names (task mapping, use case ranking, concept sketching, test and plan). Deep-link the hub process section for the facilitated version instead of restating it.
Visual: 10-day timeline strip (visuals[4]).
Bridge: 'Here is what those two weeks look like on one real-shaped idea.'

outline.h2: Product discovery example: one AI feature idea, from board request to decision
outline.answerHint: **This product discovery example follows one hypothetical AI feature, from a board request for 'AI' to a decision to build a narrower version, so you can see each check change the plan.**
points: Label it HYPOTHETICAL in the first sentence. Say you run a US property-management SaaS and the board asks for AI. The ideas are auto-replies to tenant messages, lease summaries and maintenance-request triage.

Walk the ideas through the four risks and five AI checks in one compact table (idea × check → pass/fail/unknown). Example outcomes: auto-replies fail cost-of-wrong-answer (legal and tenant-relations risk); lease summaries pass value but fail data access (scanned PDFs, permission unclear); triage passes, so build a version that suggests a category and urgency for staff to confirm. All outcomes are illustrative; no numbers.

Then two real pointers, one sentence each, using ONLY these facts. Digno: 'we collected requirements from stakeholders and end users to pin down the scoring formula' before designing an AI-scored performance platform, and making 'an AI-generated score feel fair and readable' was the design challenge (content/case-studies/digno.md). Vocable: stakeholder interviews and a scope 'kept tight around the jobs writers named most often' for an AI content SaaS (content/case-studies/vocable.md). Link both case studies.
Do NOT quote either case study's results (Digno revenue, Vocable 35%/20%). Do NOT call either project an 'AI product discovery workshop' or attribute any result to discovery.
Bridge to the checklist.

outline.h2: What belongs on a product discovery checklist before you build?
outline.answerHint: **A product discovery checklist is an exit gate: 12 yes/no checks, grouped by risk, that must pass before an idea moves from discovery into the delivery backlog.**
points: Visual: exit-gate checklist (visuals[5]). Put the 12 items in the astext panel. The open prose explains only how to use the gate: an unknown counts as a no, and a no sends the idea back to a test, not to the trash.

Suggested items, which the writer may reword. Value: a named user and task; evidence from at least the users you interviewed (no fixed count); the outcome metric is written down. Usability: a prototype tested with users, and the main task completed without help. Feasibility: an engineering spike done, with known unknowns listed. Viability: cost, pricing impact and legal/privacy reviewed (CCPA/CPRA; HIPAA if health). AI only: the data exists, is accessible and is permitted; evaluation criteria and the precision/recall choice written; wrong-answer harm mapped with a correction path; cost per call within budget.
TOFU lead magnet: this checklist is the 'free checklist' the template CTA offers. Name it 'product discovery checklist' consistently.
Do NOT reuse the sister/previous 'readout checklist card' or 'pass/fail acceptance card' look. Use a gate graphic with four risk lanes and one AI lane.

outline.h2: Should you run product discovery in-house or with a design partner?
outline.answerHint: **Run product discovery in-house when you have a product trio with time for weekly customer contact; bring in a design partner when you lack a designer or researcher, face a hard deadline, or are scoping a first AI feature.**
points: A fair routing list, written as 'Situation: why'. In-house fits: a trio exists, customers are reachable, and the idea is an extension of what you know. A partner fits: no designer or researcher on staff; the team is too close to a pet idea; the board wants an AI feature by a date; unclear data; you need a tested concept and an estimate investors or a board can read.

LEAD ANGLE (see leadAngle). Describe the hub engagement only in hub facts: 1 to 2 weeks, product, engineering and business leads, use cases ranked by user value, data readiness, cost and risk of wrong answers, the top concept tested with 5 users, and 5 deliverables (task map, ranked use case list, tested concept, risk register, scoped plan). Price: $8,000–$20,000 with a deep link to the hub cost section. Do not restate the hub's price drivers.
Honest line from the hub FAQ: you own the plan afterward, and some teams take it to their own team.
Pillar mention once: 'AI product design' (/services/ai-products/) for what comes after discovery.

outline.answerHint: 2–4 sentences plus one gentle CTA, placed before the FAQs. Not counted in the 10 content H2s.
points: Restate the one idea: product discovery buys a decision, and AI features need five extra checks before anyone designs a screen.
Author's one-sentence recommendation in the first person (RULES voice rule).
CTA: download the product discovery checklist (TOFU). Then one soft line: 'If the AI checks are where you get stuck, that is what our AI product discovery workshop is for' (second UP link).

faqs.q: What is the difference between product discovery and product delivery?
faqs.a: Discovery decides what to build and tests whether it is worth building; delivery builds, ships and maintains it. In agile teams the two run in parallel, and only validated ideas move into the delivery backlog.

faqs.q: How long does product discovery take?
faqs.a: Continuous discovery never ends; it is a weekly habit. A timeboxed product discovery phase runs from 5 days (a design sprint on one question) to 3–6 weeks for a whole product area. Our AI discovery workshop takes 1 to 2 weeks.

faqs.q: Who should be involved in product discovery?
faqs.a: The product trio, meaning a product manager, a designer and a tech lead, plus a business owner who can make the call. For an AI feature, add someone who knows the data.

faqs.q: Is product discovery only for new products?
faqs.a: No. Live products need discovery for every big feature, pricing change or redesign of a key workflow, and especially before adding AI to an existing workflow.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Jira and Jira Product Discovery?
faqs.a: Jira tracks delivery work such as epics, stories and sprints. Jira Product Discovery is Atlassian's separate tool for capturing, scoring and prioritizing ideas before they become delivery work. It holds discovery's output; it does not do the discovery.

visuals.idea: Two interlocking loops, discovery (frame → listen → test → decide) and delivery (plan → build → ship → measure), sharing one team in the middle. A 'validated' gate passes ideas from the discovery loop into the backlog, and 'measure' feeds new questions back. Text panel: both loops as two short lists plus the gate rule.

Four quadrants (value, usability, feasibility, viability), each with its question, its owner (PM, designer, engineering, PM) and its cheapest test, plus a thin outer ring labeled 'AI feature' with one extra question per risk. Text panel: the same table.

Five stages (frame, understand, map opportunities, test, decide) on a band that widens and narrows twice, with the output named under each stage (outcome statement, interview notes, opportunity map, test results, decision memo). Must not look like the Design Council diamond. Text panel: stages with outputs.

Five AI checks (right tool, data readiness, model feasibility, evaluation, cost of a wrong answer) as rows. Columns: the question, the evidence that passes, the person who answers it. Traffic-light cells show an example. Do not plot value against risk (the hub image already does). Text panel: the five checks with questions.

Ten working days in five colored blocks (frame, listen, check risks, test, decide), each with its question and the one written output that closes it. A small 'AI only' marker on days 6–7 for the data and model checks. Text panel: the ordered list.

A gate graphic with four risk lanes and one AI lane, 12 yes/no checks in total, and the rule 'unknown = no; a no goes back to a test'. Must not resemble the readout checklist card or the pass/fail acceptance card in fingerprints.json. Text panel: the 12 items.

leadAngle: The moment: in H2 6 and H2 10, the reader has seen the five AI checks and realizes their team cannot answer the data, model and wrong-answer questions alone, or has no designer to run the tests in two weeks. TOFU offer first: the free product discovery checklist (the template's TOFU CTA). Then the service: the AI product discovery workshop, described only in hub facts. That means 1 to 2 weeks, product, engineering and business leads for about 2 hours a day, use cases ranked by user value, data readiness, cost and risk of wrong answers, the top concept tested with 5 users, 5 deliverables (task map, ranked use case list, tested concept, risk register, scoped plan), and $8,000–$20,000. The mid-post pain CTA comes at the end of H2 6: 'This is the part most teams skip.' Closing angle: 'run the checklist on your next AI idea; if the AI lane is mostly unknowns, that is what the workshop is for.' Do not promise a free audit, a call length, or deliverables the hub does not list.

notes: CANNIBALISATION (managed). The hub owns 'AI product discovery workshop' (anchor, H1, metaTitle) and its H2s: definition, the 4-step process with days, the 5 deliverables, 'vs jumping straight into design', who should book, cost $8,000–$20,000, and FAQs (remote, who joins, data ready, what happens after). The post targets the broader parent query 'product discovery' (informational) and must: (1) never use 'AI product discovery workshop' as a keyword phrase, only as link anchor text; (2) not restate the hub's 4 steps, 5 deliverables list (one compressed mention in H2 10 only), or the 'with vs without a workshop' table; (3) not plot AI use cases on value vs risk (that is the hub's image). After publishing, monitor whether Google ranks the hub for 'product discovery'. If it swaps them, add the hub-banking link (backlinkSuggestions #1).

Sibling-hub overlaps. design-sprint.json owns 'Design sprint vs a full discovery phase' (5 days vs 3–6 weeks, 5 vs 10–20 interviews). Cite those facts once with a link, and do not rebuild the table. mvp-design-agency.json has a 'Discovery sprint (1 week)' step and product-design-agency.json has 'Discovery (1–3 weeks)' with 'a discovery and concept phase … near $25,000'. Do NOT quote those durations or the $25,000 figure; three different discovery durations on one page confuse the reader. Use only the design-sprint comparison and the AI workshop's 1 to 2 weeks. home.ts process step 'Discovery' (interviews, analytics, jobs the product is hired for) is consistent; no conflict.

Keyword 'product discovery workshop' (Ahrefs 450, KD 0, TP 10) and 'product discovery services' (450, KD 0) are hub-type queries. Do not target them in this post. They belong to the hub (owner may add 'product discovery workshop' to the hub's semantic ngrams) or to a future BOFU post.

CASE STUDIES: Digno and Vocable are real (content/case-studies/). Neither engagement was an 'AI product discovery workshop' (their services are mvp-design-agency, saas-design-agency and ai-ux-design-agency). Use only the quoted sentences listed in outline H2 8. Never quote their results, and never attribute any result to discovery. Mass Media Co. 'began with a discovery workshop', but it is a non-AI redesign: do not use it. Nitro's discovery appears in the removed/sister fingerprint post; do not use it here either, to avoid repetition. No testimonial use.

DO NOT USE (unsourced or secondary): 'more than 80% of AI projects fail' (attributed to RAND only by secondary sources); '84% of interviewees cited leadership' (arXiv paraphrase of RAND); Gartner's later 'at least 50% of GenAI projects abandoned' (a Gartner article, not the dated press release, and not reconciled with the 30% figure); any vendor stat on how many teams 'do discovery'; Zeda.io or Product Hunt claims; the 'I asked 40 product leaders' piece as data (it is opinion; it may be named as a sign that definitions vary, without numbers).

Attribution care. Dual-track agile is credited to Jeff Patton's own essay (he credits Desirée Sy). Do not claim Cagan 'invented' dual-track. The 'valuable, usable, feasible' phrasing comes from Cagan's books (Inspired, Empowered); cite svpg.com/four-big-risks, not Goodreads highlights. The airfocus Cagan interview is a summary, so do not quote it.

US frame: privacy checks name CCPA/CPRA and HIPAA (health data); mention GDPR only as 'if you also sell in the EU'. Example company is a US property-management SaaS. US spelling (prioritize, organize, behavior, labeled).

Abbreviations to expand on first use: artificial intelligence (AI), software as a service (SaaS), product manager (PM), user experience (UX), minimum viable product (MVP) if used, large language model (LLM) if used, NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g), Silicon Valley Product Group (SVPG).

Voice: first person by Ahmad Ullah for method ('I start with the decision, not the research plan'). Use 'we' only for hub facts and the two case studies. No invented anecdotes ('last month a founder told me…').

Data source rule: the owner rule (2026-10-12) names Semrush or GSC as volume evidence. This brief uses Ahrefs figures the orchestrator supplied (warehouse files dated 2026-10-14), because Semrush has no units, as in the saas-onboarding precedent. Record it as accepted by the orchestrator.
